passage:
Supervisor's note, Wednesday
The July rain flooded Tenzin's ground-floor flat on Monday night. He came in on Tuesday in borrowed clothes, having lost his documents and his laptop. At lunch someone muttered that he should have known better than to rent near the nala.
Nirmala put her plate down. "He rented what he could afford. Rain doesn't check who deserves it." Then she moved to practical things: she collected spare clothes from the team, helped him list which documents to apply for again, and offered her sofa for the week.
This morning she came to me with a written request: a short emergency-leave rule for staff hit by floods, so the next person doesn't have to beg for days off. I've forwarded it to HR with my support.
— Kavita, supervisor

qa.q: What did Tenzin lose in the flood?
qa.a: He lost his documents and his laptop.

qa.q: What does Nirmala's reply at lunch show about what she believes?
qa.a: It shows she feels sympathy for Tenzin rather than blame; she believes he simply rented what he could afford and the rain hit him by chance.

qa.q: Which of Nirmala's choices reaches beyond Tenzin, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Her written request for an emergency-leave rule turns one act of kindness into fairness for the whole team, so the next person hit by a flood needn't beg.

qa.q: How might Tenzin, in borrowed clothes, have felt hearing the lunch comment and then Nirmala's reply?
qa.a: The comment probably stung on top of losing so much, and Nirmala's reply may have made him feel defended rather than judged.

grounding: A supervisor sees a young woman reject blame for a flooded colleague, help practically, and push for a fair leave rule.

passage:
Thursday, 11 pm
Sachin was one of the forty let go today. Forty, in one email. He's the person who stayed late fixing other people's bugs.
By lunch the whispers had started: "He must have been on some list for a reason." I felt it too, for a second, that tidy thought: if he did something wrong, I'm safe. Then I heard Amma's voice in my head: "Beti, don't ask why; ask what he needs."
So I asked. He needed his old project files, a reference, and someone to sit with at the tea stall while he called home. I did all three.
Tonight I started a shared sheet of openings for everyone who was let go, not just my friends. Eleven names already.
Bad things land on good people. The least I can do is not add blame.
— Chandrika

qa.q: How many people were let go in the email?
qa.a: Forty were let go, in one email.

qa.q: Why did the 'tidy thought' tempt Chandrika for a second?
qa.a: If Sachin did something wrong, then Chandrika could feel safe from the same email; the thought protects her more than it explains anything.

qa.q: What choice did Chandrika make after catching that thought, and how did it help?
qa.a: She asked Sachin what he needed instead of why it happened, then got him the files, a reference and company at the tea stall.

qa.q: How might the other people who were let go see Chandrika's shared sheet?
qa.a: They may feel less alone and less judged, since the sheet treats everyone who lost a job as deserving help, not just her friends.

grounding: A young woman resists blaming a laid-off colleague, supports him practically and opens help fairly to all.

passage:
The hailstorm lasted twenty minutes and flattened Akash's whole wheat field outside the village near Bhopal. Next morning, at the tea stall, someone said, "His father fought with the temple committee. What goes around comes around." Others nodded.
Aparna, twenty-six, the agriculture extension worker, put down her glass. "The hail fell on his field and on the Rathores' field too. Did they fight with anyone?" Nobody answered.
She walked to Akash's house. He was sitting in the yard, not speaking. She didn't say it was destiny or a lesson. She said, "This was bad luck, and it's heavy. I'm here." She sat with him for an hour, then helped him photograph the damage and fill the relief form at the block office.
Back at the office, she pushed for the hailstorm survey to cover every farm in the area, not just the big ones.

qa.q: How long did the hailstorm last?
qa.a: The hailstorm lasted twenty minutes.

qa.q: What did Aparna seem to feel when she heard the tea-stall talk?
qa.a: Aparna seemed troubled and unwilling to accept the blame, which is why she put down her glass and pointed out that the hail also fell on the Rathores' field.

qa.q: What did Aparna do for Akash, and what did she do for fairness more widely?
qa.a: She sat with him and helped him photograph the damage and fill the relief form, then pushed for the survey to cover every farm, not just the big ones.

qa.q: How might Akash have experienced Aparna's visit?
qa.a: Akash, sitting silently in the yard, may have felt less alone and less judged when she called it bad luck instead of a punishment.

grounding: It shows a young worker accepting that bad things happen to good people, supporting the farmer, and working for a fairer survey.

passage:
Zeynep's little café on a side street in Lyon closed in March. The landlord sold the building and the new owner doubled the rent overnight. Zeynep had run it for four years, and every morning she remembered her regulars' orders.
At the neighbourhood meeting, one man said, "She should have seen it coming. Bad planning." Another said, "Those things don't happen to people who are careful."
Amara, twenty-five, who lived above the bakery, felt her jaw tighten. She stood up. "Zeynep was careful. She paid every bill on time. Sometimes it's just bad luck, and a bad system."
After the meeting she went to Zeynep's flat with soup and sat on the sofa with her, mostly listening.
The next week Amara started a petition asking the council for longer notice before rent increases on small shops. Zeynep signed it first, her hand shaking a little.

qa.q: How many years had Zeynep run the café?
qa.a: Zeynep had run it for four years.

qa.q: What does Amara's tightening jaw suggest she felt at the meeting?
qa.a: It suggests she felt angry and protective, disagreeing strongly with the idea that Zeynep caused her own misfortune.

qa.q: What did Amara do both to support Zeynep and to work for fairness?
qa.a: She visited with soup and mostly listened, and then started a petition asking for longer notice before rent increases on small shops.

qa.q: How might Zeynep feel hearing Amara defend her at the meeting?
qa.a: Zeynep would likely feel less alone and less ashamed, knowing someone saw her as careful and the loss as bad luck rather than a failure.

grounding: It shows a young woman accepting that bad things happen to good people, supporting a neighbour and working for a fairer rule.

passage: At the IT office in Chennai, the morning after the floods, Akash came in late, in borrowed clothes. His ground-floor flat had filled with water overnight: his books, his laptop, his mother's wedding photos, gone. By the coffee machine someone muttered, "Who rents a ground floor near the river? Should have known." Nazia, his team lead, heard it. She didn't argue at the machine. She went straight to Akash, sat with him and asked what he needed first. Then she moved his deadlines, lent him her spare laptop and started a collection for the three staff who had lost the most. That afternoon she emailed HR: could the company add an emergency leave policy for disasters, so nobody has to depend on luck or a kind lead? "Floods don't check who deserves them," she wrote. "Our rules shouldn't make it worse."

qa.q: What did Nazia lend Akash?
qa.a: Her spare laptop.

qa.q: Why did Nazia go to Akash instead of arguing at the coffee machine?
qa.a: She felt compassion for Akash and knew he needed support more than a debate about blame.

qa.q: How did Nazia both support Akash and work for fairness?
qa.a: She moved his deadlines, lent a laptop and started a collection, then asked HR for an emergency leave policy so others wouldn't depend on luck.

qa.q: How might Akash feel when Nazia asks what he needs first?
qa.a: Akash would likely feel relieved and less alone after losing so much, instead of blamed.

grounding: A young team lead supports a colleague who lost his home in floods without blame, and pushes for a fairer policy.

passage:
Dear Mahima,
I heard about the company shutting your whole department. I'm so sorry. I also heard what some people in the old group chat said, that you "should have seen it coming." Please don't carry that. You worked harder than anyone I know. Sometimes the ground just moves under good people, and it has nothing to do with what they deserve.
What can I do? I can look over your CV this weekend, I can send your name to two teams I know are hiring, or I can just come over with biryani and not talk about jobs at all. You choose.
I've also written to our alumni group asking if we can start a proper referral list for anyone who's laid off, so it isn't just about who knows whom.
With love,
Lavanya

qa.q: What did people in the old group chat say?
qa.a: That Mahima should have seen it coming.

qa.q: How does Lavanya feel about what happened to Mahima?
qa.a: Lavanya feels sad and sorry for Mahima, and protective against the blame from the group chat.

qa.q: How does Lavanya combine support with working for fairness?
qa.a: Offering help with the CV, referrals or simply company, and starting an alumni referral list so help isn't only about who knows whom.

qa.q: How might Mahima feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Mahima might feel comforted and less ashamed, with real choices of help and no blame.

grounding: A young woman writes to a laid-off friend without blame, offers support and works for a fairer referral system.

passage: Hansa, you know the tailor's shop at the corner of our market, Iqbal chacha's? It burned down last week. Wiring fault. And you know what I heard at the tea stall? "He must have done something wrong. Things like this don't happen for nothing." I was so angry I couldn't drink my tea. Iqbal chacha is the man who stitched my school uniforms for free when Papa lost his job. So this is what Sudha did. First, I went to his house with dinner and just sat with him and his wife. No speeches. Then I got four of us to help clear the shop. And then I went to the market association and asked why the wiring in that row hadn't been checked in fifteen years. They're checking every shop now. Fires don't ask who's good, Hansa. We can still fix the wires.

qa.q: What caused the fire?
qa.a: A wiring fault.

qa.q: How did Sudha feel hearing the talk at the tea stall?
qa.a: Sudha felt so angry at the blame that the tea went untouched, because Iqbal chacha had been so kind to the family.

qa.q: What three things did Sudha do?
qa.a: Sat with Iqbal chacha and his wife over dinner, got friends to help clear the shop, and pushed the market association to check the wiring in every shop.

qa.q: How might Iqbal chacha feel when Sudha simply sits with him?
qa.a: He would probably feel comforted and less alone, supported without speeches or blame.

grounding: A young woman rejects blame for a neighbour's shop fire, supports the family and presses for fairer safety checks.

passage: I worked two desks from Minakshi when the layoffs came. Darshan, from our team, was one of the twelve let go. By lunch, people were whispering: "He must have been underperforming." "They don't cut good people." I'd half thought the same, I'm ashamed to say. It made the whole thing feel less random, and less scary for the rest of us. Minakshi didn't join in. She walked straight over to Darshan's desk and helped him pack his plant and photo frame into a box. She said, loudly enough, "You were cut because the whole project was cut. Your work was good." That evening she sent him three job leads. The next week, at the team meeting, she asked the manager to explain the criteria for the cuts in writing, so nobody would be left guessing or blaming.

qa.q: How many people were let go in the layoffs?
qa.a: Twelve were let go.

qa.q: Why did Minakshi walk straight over to Darshan's desk?
qa.a: She seemed caring and firm, wanting to support him and stop the idea that he had deserved to lose his job.

qa.q: What did Minakshi do to support Darshan and push for fairness?
qa.a: She helped him pack, said his work was good, sent job leads, and asked the manager to explain the layoff criteria in writing.

qa.q: How might Darshan feel when Minakshi spoke up for him?
qa.a: Darshan probably felt less ashamed and more supported, hearing publicly that he was cut because the project was cut.

grounding: An observer describes a colleague who accepts that bad things happen to good workers, supports the one laid off, and pushes for fair criteria.

passage:
Sunday. Arohi's flat was burgled while she was at her sister's wedding. Laptop, jewellery, her grandmother's watch. A neighbour said, "Should've got a better lock." Sarika, her friend from work, arrived with dinner and sat on the floor among the mess with her. "You didn't do this. Someone else did."
Wednesday. Arohi kept blaming herself. Sarika didn't argue; she just listened, and helped her file the police report and call her insurance company. She also noticed the lane had no working street light, and the building gate never closed.
The next Saturday. Sarika had collected twenty signatures from the building and taken them to the ward office, asking for the street light to be fixed and the gate repaired. Arohi walked beside her, holding the file. "For whoever lives here next," Sarika said.

qa.q: What was stolen from Arohi's flat?
qa.a: Laptop, jewellery, her grandmother's watch.

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling on Wednesday?
qa.a: She was still blaming herself and felt guilty, as if the burglary were somehow her fault.

qa.q: What did Sarika do, and why was it a mature response?
qa.a: She supported Arohi without blame, helped with the police report and insurance, then collected signatures for a street light and gate repair to make things fairer for everyone.

qa.q: How might the neighbour's comment about the lock have affected Arohi?
qa.a: It likely added to Arohi's guilt, suggesting the burglary was her own fault.

grounding: Shows a mature friend accepting that bad things happen to good people, supporting the victim of a burglary, and working to make the lane safer.

passage: Abhinav, you asked why I get angry when people say someone "deserved" their bad luck. Let your Damini Maasi tell you. When I was twenty-five, in Jabalpur, my neighbour Kusum's husband was hit by a truck on the highway. A good man, honest, kind to every child in the lane. At the funeral, I heard an old woman whisper, "Must be the sins of a past life." Kusum heard it too. Her face changed. Something in me said, no. I sat with Kusum every evening for a month. I didn't give her reasons. I just held her hand. And then I did one more thing. That turning had killed three people in two years. I went with the other women to the collector's office, again and again, until they put in a speed breaker and a light. Nobody deserved that road.

qa.q: What did the old woman whisper at the funeral?
qa.a: "Must be the sins of a past life."

qa.q: What was young Damini feeling when she heard the whisper?
qa.a: She felt a strong, protective anger, refusing to let Kusum's grief be turned into blame.

qa.q: Which choice in the story showed compassion and fairness together?
qa.a: Sitting with Kusum every evening without giving reasons, and going to the collector's office until a speed breaker and a light were put in.

qa.q: How might Kusum have felt when she heard the whisper?
qa.a: Kusum's face changed, suggesting she felt wounded and ashamed on top of her grief.

grounding: An elder recalls supporting a grieving neighbour without blame, accepting that bad things happen to good people, and working to fix a dangerous road.

passage:
The power had been out for six hours when Sarika waded down the lane with two torches and a bucket.
Nazia's tailoring shop sat a step lower than the others, and the water had come in to the height of the sewing machines. Nazia stood in the doorway holding a ruined roll of wedding silk.
"Everyone's saying I should have moved things up," she said. "That I was careless."
"The drain on this corner has been blocked since April," Sarika said. "It flooded the chemist too, and he's been here thirty years."
They worked by torchlight, wringing out fabric and stacking wet orders on the counter. Sarika didn't offer lessons. She asked which customers needed calling first, and wrote a list.
Before leaving, she photographed the choked drain. At home, with her phone on four percent, she typed a complaint to the ward office, and the next morning got two other shopkeepers to sign it.

qa.q: Since when had the corner drain been blocked?
qa.a: The drain on the corner had been blocked since April.

qa.q: Why did Sarika mention the chemist?
qa.a: Sarika wanted to lift Nazia's shame, and felt protective of her, by showing the flood hit a careful, long-standing shopkeeper too, so it wasn't a punishment for being careless.

qa.q: How does Sarika work for fairness beyond helping that night?
qa.a: Sarika photographs the blocked drain, sends a complaint to the ward office and gets two shopkeepers to sign it, aiming to stop the next flood.

qa.q: What is it like for Nazia when Sarika asks which customers to call first?
qa.a: Nazia likely feels steadier and less alone, because the talk moves from blame to practical next steps.

grounding: Shows a young adult who helps a flooded shopkeeper without blaming her and then pushes the ward office to fix the cause.

passage:
The Monday after the layoffs, the Gurugram office was quieter than a library. Harish's desk had already been cleared down to a single cable.
At the coffee machine, someone murmured, "They don't cut the good ones. He must have been slacking."
Disha remembered Harish staying till eleven for the client launch in March. She didn't argue with the machine. She went outside and called him.
"You don't have to say anything wise," Harish said, his voice flat. "Everyone's asking what I did wrong."
"You didn't do anything wrong. Half the payments team went too, including our best reviewer. Sometimes it just falls where it falls." She paused. "Send me your CV tonight. I'll forward it to three people I know."
That afternoon she wrote to HR, politely, asking the company to share how people had been chosen, so rumours like the one at the coffee machine would have less to feed on.

qa.q: What was left on Harish's desk the Monday after the layoffs?
qa.a: Harish's desk had been cleared down to a single cable.

qa.q: Why did Disha call Harish instead of arguing at the coffee machine?
qa.a: Disha felt uneasy about the rumour but cared more that Harish, who had stayed till eleven for the launch, felt supported than about winning an argument.

qa.q: What step could stop rumours like the one at the coffee machine?
qa.a: Asking HR to share how people were chosen, as Disha does, gives facts to replace guesses about who was slacking.

qa.q: What is it like for Harish to hear that everyone is asking what he did wrong?
qa.a: Harish feels flat and blamed, carrying shame on top of losing his job, which is why Disha's plain 'you didn't do anything wrong' matters.

grounding: Shows a young professional who accepts that a layoff can hit a hard worker, supports him without blame and asks the company for fair, open criteria.

"Mausi says I must have filled the form wrong," Chandrika said, dropping onto the sofa. "Papa agrees. Apparently I'm careless."
Binita put down the rotis. "Did you fill it wrong?"
"No! The portal crashed on the last day. My payment went through, the form didn't."
"Then it's not careless. It's a crash."
"Try telling them that." Chandrika pressed her palms against her eyes. "I studied a whole year for this scholarship."
"I know. I watched you." Binita sat down beside her. "It's rotten, and you didn't earn it. Can I see the screenshots?"
Chandrika scrolled. "There. Error at 11:52."
"Good, you kept them. Hundreds of people must have hit the same crash. Tomorrow morning I'll help you write to the scholarship office, and let's find the others online and write together."
"And Mausi?"
"Mausi can have her tea. I'll tell her about the portal myself."

qa.q: At what time did the error appear in Chandrika's screenshot?
qa.a: The error appeared at 11:52.

qa.q: What might Binita be feeling when she says 'I watched you'?
qa.a: Binita feels protective and sad for Chandrika, and wants her to know the year of effort was seen, so the crash doesn't feel like a verdict on her.

qa.q: Which of Binita's steps goes beyond comfort?
qa.a: Asking for the screenshots, planning to write to the scholarship office and finding others hit by the same crash works toward a fair fix, not just sympathy.

qa.q: How does Chandrika see the family's comment that she was careless?
qa.a: Chandrika feels unfairly blamed and deflated, since the portal crashed after a whole year of study.

grounding: Shows a young woman who supports a family member without blame after bad luck and still works with others to get it put right.

passage: When the layoffs came last June, Sangeeta was on the list. She had trained half our team, including me. By lunch, someone in the pantry was saying, "There must be a reason. They don't cut good people." I felt the pull of that idea too; it's comforting to think the world only punishes mistakes. But I had seen her work. Sometimes a whole project gets cut, and the best person on it goes with it. So I didn't try to explain it. I sat with her on the office steps while she cried, then helped her pack her plants. She hugged me and said, "Ankita, you didn't have to." That evening I wrote her a detailed reference. The next week I asked our manager, in writing, why the layoff criteria hadn't been shared, and three colleagues signed with me. We got the criteria in July. It didn't bring Sangeeta back, but the next list came with reasons.

qa.q: What did someone in the pantry say about the layoffs?
qa.a: "There must be a reason. They don't cut good people."

qa.q: What did Ankita feel on hearing the pantry comment?
qa.a: Ankita felt the comforting pull of believing only mistakes get punished, but was uneasy and unconvinced, having seen Sangeeta's work.

qa.q: Which of Ankita's actions balanced support and fairness?
qa.a: Sitting with Sangeeta and writing a reference gave support, and asking in writing for the layoff criteria worked for fairness for the next list.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta have felt when Ankita sat with her on the steps?
qa.a: Sangeeta probably felt comforted and less alone, since Ankita was not trying to explain the layoff as her fault.

grounding: Shows a person accepting that bad things happen to good people, supporting a laid-off colleague and still pushing for fairness.
